<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose
   - LeetHub 2.0 is a browser extension (Chrome & Firefox) whose goal is to automatically sync your LeetCode submissions to a GitHub repository whenever you pass all tests. It injects scripts into the LeetCode UI, captures your code, and uses the GitHub API (via OAuth2) to push commits.

2. File Structure Analysis
   - Top-level artifacts:
     • manifest-chrome.json / manifest-firefox.json – extension metadata  
     • popup.html, welcome.html (+ CSS under css/) – the extension’s UI pages  
     • scripts/ – JavaScript for background, OAuth, content-scripts and popup logic  
     • assets/extension/ – icons and images used by the extension  
     • webpack.config.js – bundling configuration to produce ./dist  
     • spec/ – Jasmine unit tests for core logic  
   - Key script groups:
     • Content Scripts (scripts/authorize.js, scripts/gfg.js, scripts/leetcode/*.js)  
     • Background Script (scripts/background.js, scripts/oauth2.js)  
     • Popup Logic (scripts/popup.js) and Welcome Logic (scripts/welcome.js)

3. README Insights
   - Describes user flow: install → authorize GitHub → select or create a repo → LeetCode page injection → auto-push on successful submissions.
   - Mentions build pipeline (npm scripts, Webpack) but focuses on runtime behavior of the extension.

4. Constructing the System Design Diagram
   a. Main Components
      1. Browser Extension Shell (defined by manifest)  
      2. UI Pages (Popup & Welcome)  
      3. Content Scripts (LeetCode & GFG injection)  
      4. Background Service Worker  
      5. OAuth2 & GitHub API  
      6. Webpack Bundler (build-time component, optional in runtime view)
   b. Relationships & Data Flows
      - UI Pages ←→ Background: popup actions (authorize, configure repo) via chrome.runtime messaging  
      - Content Scripts ←→ Background: code extraction and “submit” events via chrome.runtime messaging  
      - Background → GitHub API: HTTP calls with OAuth2 token to create commits in the user’s repo  
      - Content Scripts → LeetCode page DOM: read problem title, code, test status  
   c. Architectural Patterns
      - Event-driven message passing (Chrome extension MV3 style with service worker)  
      - Separation of concerns: UI (popup), injection (content), orchestration/persistence (background)  
   d. Key Technologies
      - Chrome/Firefox Extension APIs (manifest v2/v3)  
      - OAuth2 for GitHub authentication  
      - Webpack for bundling source → dist  
      - Jasmine for unit testing

5. Tailoring the Diagram for a Browser Extension
   - Emphasize the MV3-like separation:
     • Manifest (configuration)  
     • Service Worker (background.js)  
     • UI Panels (popup.html, welcome.html)  
     • Content Scripts (injected into LeetCode or GFG pages)  
     • External Endpoints (GitHub API, LeetCode site)  
   - Show build pipeline as a side note or footnote, not core to runtime behavior.

6. Diagramming Guidelines
   - Use clear labels:
     • Boxes for each component, e.g., “Popup UI”, “Background Service Worker”, “Content Script”  
     • Note file examples under each box for clarity (e.g., content script: scripts/leetcode/leetcode.js)  
   - Use directional arrows:
     • UI → Background (user actions)  
     • Background → GitHub API (HTTP commit)  
     • Content Script → Background (message: code ready)  
     • Content Script ↔ LeetCode DOM (inject & read)  
   - Color-code or shape-code:
     • UI components in one color (e.g., green)  
     • Scripts/service worker in another (e.g., blue)  
     • External services in a third (e.g., red)  
   - Optionally annotate messaging channels (chrome.runtime.sendMessage) and storage (chrome.storage).

7. Final Tips
   - Capture every logical boundary: browser host vs. extension sandbox vs. external services.  
   - Don’t overcomplicate: each script folder becomes one logical component.  
   - Call out the OAuth2 handshake as a distinct flow in the diagram.  
   - Ensure arrows indicate data direction (e.g., “push code → GitHub”).  

By following this breakdown, you’ll produce a system design diagram that clearly reflects LeetHub’s architecture: manifest-driven extension that injects content, orchestrates via a background service worker, and integrates with GitHub over OAuth2, all wrapped in a build pipeline powered by Webpack and verified by Jasmine tests.
</explanation>
